fact.slime.glow.junior: Glow powder soaks up light and gives it back slowly, so it shines in the dark! Real glow-in-the-dark toys work the same way.
fact.slime.glow.expert: Glow-in-the-dark materials are phosphorescent: they absorb light energy and release it slowly as visible light. Glow powder is (mostly) real; magic slime is just for fun!

fact.slime.bouncy.junior: Slime is a polymer: lots of long, wiggly chains linked together. More links make it bouncier!
fact.slime.bouncy.expert: Slime is a cross-linked polymer. More cross-links between the long chains make it springier, so it bounces instead of splatting.

fact.slime.rainbow.junior: White light is really all the colors of the rainbow mixed together!
fact.slime.rainbow.expert: White light contains every visible wavelength. A prism or raindrop bends each color a different amount, splitting light into a rainbow.

fact.slime.stretchy.junior: Stretchy slime acts like a liquid AND a solid. Pull it slowly and it stretches. Pull it fast and it snaps!
fact.slime.stretchy.expert: Slime is non-Newtonian: how runny it is depends on how fast you push or pull it. Slow pulls let polymer chains slide; fast pulls make them snap.

fact.circuit.paperclip.junior: Paperclips are made of metal, and metal lets electricity flow through it. That makes it a conductor!
fact.circuit.paperclip.expert: Metals have free electrons that move easily, so steel paperclips conduct electricity.

fact.circuit.coin.junior: Coins are metal, so electricity zooms right through them!
fact.circuit.coin.expert: Coins are metal alloys like copper and nickel, which are good electrical conductors.

fact.circuit.foil.junior: Foil is a very thin sheet of aluminum metal. It's a great conductor!
fact.circuit.foil.expert: Aluminum foil conducts well because aluminum is a metal with lots of free electrons.

fact.circuit.rubber_band.junior: Rubber stops electricity. That's called an insulator! Wires are covered in rubber or plastic to keep us safe.
fact.circuit.rubber_band.expert: Rubber is an insulator: its electrons are held tightly and can't flow, which is why wires are coated in rubber or plastic.

fact.circuit.plastic_spoon.junior: Plastic is an insulator, so the bulb stays dark.
fact.circuit.plastic_spoon.expert: Plastics are insulators. They don't let electric current flow, so the circuit stays open.

fact.circuit.wood_stick.junior: Dry wood doesn't let electricity through. It's an insulator!
fact.circuit.wood_stick.expert: Dry wood is a poor conductor. Wet wood conducts a little, because of the water and salts inside it.

fact.circuit.pencil.junior: Surprise! Pencil lead is made of graphite, and graphite conducts electricity, even though it isn't a metal!
fact.circuit.pencil.expert: Graphite (pencil 'lead') is carbon arranged in layers with free electrons, so it conducts electricity even though it's not a metal.

fact.circuit.key.junior: Keys are made of metal, so they conduct electricity.
fact.circuit.key.expert: Most keys are brass, a copper-zinc alloy, which conducts electricity well.

fact.circuit.eraser.junior: Erasers are rubber, and rubber is an insulator. No light!
fact.circuit.eraser.expert: Erasers are made of rubber or vinyl, both insulators.

fact.circuit.marble.junior: Glass is an insulator. Electricity can't get through a marble!
fact.circuit.marble.expert: Glass is an excellent insulator at room temperature, which is why it's used on power lines.

fact.micro.pond.junior: A drop of pond water is full of tiny living things, too small to see without a microscope!
fact.micro.pond.expert: Pond water holds microorganisms like paramecia, which swim using tiny hairs called cilia.

fact.micro.leaf.junior: Leaves are made of tiny boxes called cells. The green dots inside help the plant make food from sunlight!
fact.micro.leaf.expert: Leaf cells contain chloroplasts, which use sunlight to make sugar through photosynthesis.

fact.micro.hair.junior: Up close, a hair is covered in tiny overlapping scales, like the shingles on a roof!
fact.micro.hair.expert: Hair has an outer layer called the cuticle, made of overlapping scales of keratin.

fact.micro.onion.junior: Onion skin cells look like little bricks stacked in a wall. Each has a dot inside called the nucleus!
fact.micro.onion.expert: Onion epidermis cells are easy to see because they're large and flat. The dark spot in each is the nucleus, which holds the cell's DNA.

fact.micro.salt.junior: Every grain of salt is a tiny cube! Salt crystals grow in cube shapes.
fact.micro.salt.expert: Table salt (sodium chloride) forms cubic crystals because of how its atoms stack together.

fact.micro.sand.junior: Sand is made of teeny tiny rocks, broken down over a very long time by wind and water!
fact.micro.sand.expert: Sand grains are mostly quartz, worn down from bigger rocks by weathering and erosion over thousands of years.

fact.micro.wing.junior: Butterfly wings are covered in thousands of tiny colored scales, like a mosaic!
fact.micro.wing.expert: Butterfly wings are covered in tiny scales. Some colors come from pigments, and some from structures that bend light.

fact.gravity.moon.junior: The Moon has much weaker gravity than Earth, so you can jump about 6 times higher there!
fact.gravity.moon.expert: Moon gravity is 1.62 m/s², about 1/6 of Earth's. The same jump goes about six times higher.

fact.gravity.mars.junior: Mars gravity is a bit more than one third of Earth's. You'd be a super jumper there!
fact.gravity.mars.expert: Mars surface gravity is 3.71 m/s², about 38% of Earth's.

fact.gravity.earth.junior: Earth's gravity keeps our feet on the ground and pulls everything down at the same speed, heavy or light!
fact.gravity.earth.expert: Earth's gravity is 9.81 m/s². Without air, a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate. Astronauts tested this on the Moon!

fact.gravity.jupiter.junior: Jupiter's gravity is so strong you could hardly jump at all! It's the biggest planet.
fact.gravity.jupiter.expert: Jupiter's gravity at its cloud tops is 24.79 m/s², about 2.5 times Earth's. (It has no solid surface to stand on!)

fact.gravity.pluto.junior: Pluto is tiny, so its gravity is super weak. You could jump higher than a basketball hoop!
fact.gravity.pluto.expert: Pluto's gravity is just 0.62 m/s², about 1/16 of Earth's.

crystal.hint.weak.junior: Not enough powder! The water has to be FULL of powder before crystals can grow. Add more spoons.
crystal.hint.weak.expert: The solution isn't saturated. Crystals only grow when the water holds as much powder as it can. Add more.

crystal.hint.cold.junior: Cold water can't hold that much! Try hot water. It dissolves lots more.
crystal.hint.cold.expert: Solubility goes up with temperature. Dissolve it in hot water, then crystals form as it cools.

crystal.hint.pile.junior: Too much! Some powder won't dissolve and just sits in a pile. Use fewer spoons.
crystal.hint.pile.expert: Past saturation, extra powder stays undissolved at the bottom. Use fewer spoons.

gforce.hint.junior: Try every ride and watch the g-meter. The bigger the number, the harder you get squished!
gforce.hint.expert: Felt weight = mass x g-force. Try the roller coaster and read the meter.

garden.hint.soggy.junior: Too much water! The roots got soggy. One splash a day is plenty.
garden.hint.soggy.expert: Waterlogged soil has no air, and roots need oxygen too. Water a little each day.

fact.crystal.salt.junior: Salt crystals are tiny cubes! Look at table salt with a magnifier and you'll see little boxes.
fact.crystal.salt.expert: Sodium and chloride stack in a cube-shaped pattern, so salt crystals grow as cubes. Salt dissolves about the same hot or cold, so salt crystals mostly grow as water evaporates.

fact.crystal.sugar.junior: Rock candy is one big sugar crystal! Hot water holds tons of sugar, and as it cools the sugar sticks together into crystals.
fact.crystal.sugar.expert: Hot water dissolves more than twice as much sugar as cold water. As the syrup cools, sugar comes out of solution and builds crystals.

fact.crystal.alum.junior: Alum crystals look like two pyramids stuck together. Sparkly!
fact.crystal.alum.expert: Alum forms octahedral crystals with eight triangle faces. It dissolves much better in hot water, so it's great for growing big crystals.

fact.crystal.epsom.junior: Epsom salt grows long, thin, spiky crystals like needles!
fact.crystal.epsom.expert: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate. When it crystallizes quickly, it makes long needle-shaped crystals.

fact.gforce.still.junior: Sitting still on Earth, you feel 1 g. That's just your normal weight!
fact.gforce.still.expert: 1 g is the push you feel from Earth's gravity, 9.81 m/s². G-force compares any push to that.

fact.gforce.elevator.junior: When an elevator starts going up, you feel a tiny bit heavier for a moment!
fact.gforce.elevator.expert: Speeding up upward adds to gravity's pull, so an elevator starting up can make you feel about 1.2 g.

fact.gforce.rocket.junior: Astronauts get pressed into their seats at launch with about 3 times their weight!
fact.gforce.rocket.expert: The Space Shuttle kept launches to about 3 g so astronauts stayed safe. Lying on their backs helped too.

fact.gforce.coaster.junior: At the bottom of a big loop, a roller coaster pushes on you with about 4 times your weight!
fact.gforce.coaster.expert: At the bottom of a loop the track pushes you up hard to curve your path. Big coasters reach 4 to 5 g for a moment.

fact.gforce.jet.junior: Fighter pilots can feel 9 g in a tight turn! They wear special suits to keep blood in their heads.
fact.gforce.jet.expert: At 9 g, blood is pulled toward the feet. Pilots wear g-suits that squeeze their legs and use special breathing to avoid blacking out.

fact.trivia.sun.junior: The Sun is a star! It's the closest star to Earth, so it looks much bigger and brighter than the others.
fact.trivia.sun.expert: The Sun is a medium-sized star about 109 times wider than Earth. Other stars look tiny because they're so far away.

fact.trivia.red_planet.junior: Mars is red because its dirt has rusty iron in it!
fact.trivia.red_planet.expert: Mars is covered in iron oxide (rust) dust, which gives it its red color.

fact.trivia.biggest.junior: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it!
fact.trivia.biggest.expert: Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth. Over 1,300 Earths could fit inside.

fact.trivia.rings.junior: Saturn's rings are made of chunks of ice and rock. Some are tiny like dust and some are as big as houses!
fact.trivia.rings.expert: Saturn's rings are billions of ice and rock pieces. They're super wide but very thin compared to how wide they are.

fact.trivia.planets.junior: There are 8 planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune!
fact.trivia.planets.expert: There are 8 planets. Pluto was called a planet until 2006, when scientists renamed it a dwarf planet.

fact.trivia.closest.junior: Mercury is closest to the Sun, and it zooms all the way around it in just 88 days!
fact.trivia.closest.expert: Mercury orbits the Sun every 88 Earth days, faster than any other planet.

fact.trivia.moonlight.junior: The Moon doesn't glow by itself. Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off the Moon!
fact.trivia.moonlight.expert: The Moon reflects sunlight. Its phases are how much of its sunlit side we can see from Earth.

fact.trivia.hottest.junior: Venus is hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun! Venus's thick clouds trap heat like a blanket.
fact.trivia.hottest.expert: Venus's thick carbon dioxide air causes a runaway greenhouse effect. Its surface is about 465 °C, hot enough to melt lead.

fact.trivia.light_time.junior: Light is the fastest thing there is, but the Sun is so far away that its light takes about 8 minutes to get here!
fact.trivia.light_time.expert: Light travels about 300,000 km every second. The Sun is about 150 million km away, so sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds.

fact.trivia.venus_day.junior: Venus spins so slowly that one spin takes 243 Earth days, but it goes around the Sun in just 225!
fact.trivia.venus_day.expert: Venus rotates once every 243 Earth days (backwards!) and orbits the Sun every 225 days.

fact.trivia.volcano.junior: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano we know. It's about 2 and a half times taller than Mount Everest!
fact.trivia.volcano.expert: Olympus Mons is about 22 km tall. Mars has weak gravity and no moving plates, so the volcano kept growing in one spot.

fact.trivia.black_hole.junior: A black hole's gravity is so strong that nothing can get out, not even light. That's why it's black!
fact.trivia.black_hole.expert: Inside the event horizon, escape would need to go faster than light, which nothing can do.

fact.garden.sunflower.junior: Young sunflowers turn to follow the Sun across the sky!
fact.garden.sunflower.expert: Young sunflowers track the Sun from east to west each day. Grown-up flowers mostly stay facing east.

fact.garden.tulip.junior: Tulips grow from bulbs. A bulb stores food underground, like a packed lunch for the plant!
fact.garden.tulip.expert: A tulip bulb is an underground stem packed with stored food, so the plant can sprout quickly in spring.

fact.garden.rose.junior: Roses have prickles to keep hungry animals from eating them.
fact.garden.rose.expert: Rose 'thorns' are really prickles that grow from the stem's skin. Roses are cousins of apples and strawberries!

fact.garden.daisy.junior: A daisy is really lots of tiny flowers packed together! The yellow middle is full of them.
fact.garden.daisy.expert: Daisies are composite flowers: the yellow center is many tiny disc florets, and each white 'petal' is a ray floret.

fact.garden.full.junior: Gardens help bees and butterflies! They drink nectar and carry pollen from flower to flower.
fact.garden.full.expert: Pollinators like bees carry pollen between flowers so plants can make seeds. Lots of the food we eat depends on them.

fact.robot.floor.junior: Wheels roll smoothly on flat floors, so they're super fast and use little energy.
fact.robot.floor.expert: On hard, flat ground wheels have very little rolling resistance, which makes them the most efficient way to move.

fact.robot.sand.junior: Tank tracks spread the robot's weight over a big area, so it doesn't sink into soft sand.
fact.robot.sand.expert: Tracks lower ground pressure by spreading weight over a large area. That's why bulldozers use them on soft ground.

fact.robot.stairs.junior: Legs can step up and over things that wheels just bump into!
fact.robot.stairs.expert: Legged robots handle stairs and rough ground, but balancing is hard. They use sensors and fast computers to stay upright.

fact.robot.cave.junior: Bats find their way in the dark using sound echoes. Robots can too, with sonar!
fact.robot.cave.expert: Sonar sends out sound pulses and times the echoes to measure distance. It works in total darkness, where cameras can't see.

fact.robot.junkyard.junior: Magnets pull on iron and steel, so a magnet arm can grab bolts without even seeing them!
fact.robot.junkyard.expert: Iron, nickel, and cobalt are magnetic. Recycling centers use giant electromagnets to pull steel out of the trash.
